title: The prince with no equal
hook: Satyavati's proud son thinks no one is his equal, and Hindu teaching has a name for that
carry: ahamkara: the ego that says no equal

segments.voice: Yesterday, Satyavati in the boat, and her island-born son Vyasa. Guru Purnima thanks Vyasa and every teacher.

Two warriors face each other, and they share a name. One is a prince of the Kurus. The other is a powerful king of the Gandharvas, the heavenly musicians. The text calls them namesakes, and says the Gandharva came looking for this fight. That's how the story of Satyavati's first son ends. To get there, go back to the palace, where the fisherman's daughter is now a queen.
screen: `TWO WARRIORS, ONE NAME.` → `THE GANDHARVA COMES TO FIGHT.`

segments.voice: Satyavati has married King Shantanu on the terms Bhishma's vow made possible. She bears him two sons, Chitrangada and then Vichitravirya. Before the younger is grown, Shantanu dies. Bhishma keeps his word: he places Chitrangada on the throne and answers to Satyavati as his mother. Chitrangada is strong, and the text says he's proud. He defeats king after king, and comes to think no one is his equal. That's when the Gandharva of the same name arrives, looking for this fight. They fight at Kurukshetra, beside the Sarasvati, long and hard, and the Gandharva, with the illusions of his kind, kills the prince. Bhishma performs the funeral rites, and sets the boy Vichitravirya on the throne. The poem gives Satyavati no speech; her grief stays quiet. Now the teaching. Hindu thought has a name for what grew in Chitrangada: ahamkara, literally the I-maker. It's the voice that says, I did this, I'm the best, no one's my equal. The Bhagavad Gita, spoken later on this same field of Kurukshetra, says the one deluded by ahamkara thinks, I am the doer, when it's nature doing the work, and it lists pride and arrogance among the marks of a demonic nature. It isn't a rule against being good at things. Chitrangada really did win. The trouble was the story he told himself about it. That's why many Hindus end a puja by offering it back, some saying Krishnarpanam, given to Krishna, and why touching an elder's feet is a small, daily bow of the I.
screen: `A PROUD SON ON THE THRONE.` · `THE FIGHT AT KURUKSHETRA.` · `AHAMKARA: THE I-MAKER.` · `THE GITA ON PRIDE.` · then, large: `OFFER THE WIN BACK.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you did well lately. Hold it and enjoy it; that's allowed. Then, the way many Hindus close a prayer, set it down: fold your hands and bow your head. If you pray, offer it to God, in your own words. If you don't, thank the people, the teachers and the luck that helped. Notice that the win is still yours, and lighter.
Satyavati. A widowed queen with one son lost to his own pride and his namesake, and one boy left on the throne.
Your line: ahamkara, the ego that says no equal. A boy king, a queen mother and a vow now hold the house. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Hindus end a puja by offering the worship and its fruits back to God, some with the words 'Krishnarpanam astu', may it be an offering to Krishna; touching an elder's feet is another everyday bow of the ego.

Kurukshetra.meaning: the field where Chitrangada fell, and where the Gita is spoken

Sarasvati.meaning: the river beside which the namesakes fought

Chitrangada.meaning: Satyavati's proud elder son, killed by his namesake

Vichitravirya.meaning: Satyavati's younger son, crowned as a boy

ahamkara.meaning: the ego, the 'I-maker' that claims to be the only doer

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (the sons of Satyavati; Shantanu's death; Chitrangada slain by the Gandharva Chitrangada; Vichitravirya installed)
Bhagavad Gita 3.27 (deluded by ahamkara, one thinks 'I am the doer')
Bhagavad Gita 16.4 (pride and arrogance among the demonic traits)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli: Shantanu dies before Vichitravirya comes of age; Bhishma installs Chitrangada and obeys Satyavati; the Gandharva's challenge over the shared name; the fight at Kurukshetra on the Sarasvati; the Gandharva's use of illusion; Bhishma performs the rites and rules for the boy Vichitravirya.
The length of the fight is given in the text as a number of years; it is left out under the claims rule.
The two readings of Satyavati's silence are unattributed and unranked.
howItsDone generalizes about funeral rites ('often'); a Keeper may prefer different wording.
